newsitem.title: UK: Major insists British beef is safe.
newsitem.headline: Major insists British beef is safe.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major insisted on Thursday that meat from British cattle was safe to eat despite fresh evidence from scientists that people can get a new human form of mad cow disease from beef.

The scientists' report is expected to rock already shaky consumer confidence. But Major said there was no justification for the European Union to harden its stance against lifting its global ban on British beef exports because of the new development.

"There's no new fresh public health concern. People can eat beef as safely today as they could yesterday, and I think it's perfectly safe," Major told BBC television. "There is no need for the European Union to panic and change its views."

He was backed by John Pattison, the government's senior scientific adviser on mad cow disease -- Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) -- who said he personally would have no reservations about eating British beef.
"All the necessary restrictions on (contaminated) British beef going into the human food chain are now in place," he told BBC radio.

British officials said Britain took measures as long ago as 1989 to prevent cattle from eating feed containing the remains of other mammals, thought to be the original cause of BSE, and had tightened up other controls more recently.
But Gerald Kiely, a European Union agriculture spokesman, said the new research justified the cautious attitude the EU had taken on allowing British beef into the markets of other states.

"The result of this research in the U.K. confirms that the Commission was prudent in all of the actions it took relating to BSE and in assuming there could be a link between BSE and CJD (the human version, Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease)," he said.
The European Union banned exports after British ministers disclosed in March that there was a probable link between the eating of beef from cattle in the early stages of BSE and a new variant of CJD.
The news caused beef sales in Britain to fall to just over 70 percent of normal. They have now recovered to 85 percent.
After agreeing to a cull of thousands of vulnerable cattle, Major got an agreement in June from fellow EU heads of government to a phased lifting of the ban.

Since then, Britain has declared that part of this cull is unnecessary and no progress has been made in allowing British exports to resume despite angry protests from farmers that their businesses are in crisis.

The new research, by John Collinge of London's Imperial College of Science and Medicine and scientists at the National CJD Surveillance Unit, shows that CJD leaves a clear chemical signature that is very similar to BSE.
"This provides supportive evidence for BSE being the cause of new variant CJD," Collinge said.
The evidence was a potential embarrassment for officials of Britain's Meat and Livestock Commission, who were launching a Festival of British Beef in London on Thursday.
But Colin Maclean, the director-general of the trade organisation, said: "So far as the safety of British beef is concerned, this research has no implications."

The National Farmers Union said in a statement: "There is no cause for consumers to be alarmed. All the controls that have been in place since 1989 were put in place on the assumption that BSE was connected to human health."
